issues.legal_issue: A record of possession-taking does not establish that acquired land vested in the government when the land remained cultivated and the record shows only paper possession.
material_facts: The owner continued cultivating the acquired land, and unchallenged cultivation records showed crops on it at the time possession was said to have been taken.
The authorities relied on a record of delivery of possession, but produced no evidence of actual possession-taking in the presence of the cultivator or independent witnesses.
The owner challenged the acquisition in a writ petition, which the High Court dismissed on the ground that possession had been taken and the land had vested in the government.
issues.conclusion: The record prepared by the authorities did not establish that possession had been taken or that the land had vested in the government. The High Court erred in dismissing the writ petition on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 16 and 17(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, vesting requires actual possession, not possession merely on paper or symbolic possession as understood in civil proceedings. The mode of taking possession depends on the nature of the land. Balwant Narayan Bhagde v. M. D. Bhagwat held that possession must be actual and the method depends on the land; Banda Development Authority v. Moti Lal Agarwal summarized that where crops or structures exist, merely going to the site is ordinarily insufficient, and notice and possession in the presence of independent witnesses will ordinarily be required. The Court distinguished Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Industrial Development and Investment Company, Star Wire (India) Ltd. v. State of Haryana, C. Padma v. Deputy Secretary to the Government of Tamil Nadu, Municipal Council, Ahmednagar v. Shah Hyder Beig, and Swaika Properties (P) Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan, which involved delay and did not address the legality of the possession-taking method in this case.

rule.if: acquisition_writ_challenge and crops_standing and cultivation_records_unrebutted and (possession_record_only or not evidence_of_actual_possession)

predicates.acquisition_writ_challenge: An affected landholder sought judicial review of a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.crops_standing: Crops were growing on the land when the authorities claimed to take possession.
predicates.cultivation_records_unrebutted: Records showed that the landholder continued cultivating the land, and the opposing authority did not challenge those records.
predicates.possession_record_only: The authority relied on a document recording delivery of possession rather than evidence demonstrating an actual taking of possession.
predicates.evidence_of_actual_possession: The authority produced evidence that actual possession was taken from the cultivator.

issues.definition: When a landholder challenges a compulsory acquisition, crops remain on the land, cultivation records remain unrebutted, and the authority relies only on a possession document or lacks evidence of actual possession, the paper record does not establish vesting.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to give a landholder a fair opportunity to be heard on an objection to compulsory acquisition invalidates the acquisition.
material_facts: The landholder filed an objection to the proposed acquisition.
The notices allegedly issued to the landholder and his wife did not bear their signatures acknowledging receipt, and the authorities offered no explanation for this.
The record showed a signature attributed to the landholder at the hearing, but the Court found it did not match his signatures on court documents; the authorities could not explain the discrepancy.
The acquisition officer proceeded on the assumption that notice had been delivered and did not provide the landholder an opportunity to be heard.
issues.conclusion: The landholder was not given the required opportunity of hearing. The acquisition of his land was illegal and was quashed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5A(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires the Collector to give an objector an opportunity to be heard, consider the objections, make further inquiry, and report recommendations to the appropriate government. The hearing embodies natural justice and must be fair; the recommendations must reflect objective consideration of the objections and brief reasons. Munshi Singh v. Union of India described the hearing and reporting duties; State of Punjab v. Gurdial Singh emphasized the need for a hearing before compulsory deprivation of property; and Shyam Nandan Prasad v. State of Bihar held compliance with Section 5A to be essential to valid acquisition. The Court also relied on Union of India v. Mukesh Hans, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Darius Shapur Chenai, Anand Singh v. State of U.P., and Radhy Shyam v. State of U.P.

rule.if: acquisition_objection_challenge and landholder_filed_objection and notice_not_served and hearing_not_provided

predicates.acquisition_objection_challenge: A landholder challenged a compulsory acquisition on the basis of the process used to consider an objection.
predicates.landholder_filed_objection: The landholder submitted an objection to the proposed acquisition.
predicates.notice_not_served: The authority did not serve the landholder with notice of the objection hearing.
predicates.hearing_not_provided: The authority decided the objection without giving the landholder an opportunity to present it.

issues.definition: When a landholder challenges the objection process, has filed an objection, was not served with notice, and was not given a hearing, the acquisition is invalid.
